Holiday Club Scam UK: How to Spot and Avoid Timeshare Fraud

Holiday club scams promise the world but deliver debt — here's how to recognise and avoid them.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-07-05 · Updated 2026-07-30 · 10 min read

Quick answer: A holiday club that pressures you to sign an expensive long-term membership at a presentation is a warning sign — genuine costs and cancellation terms should be in writing first. Do not sign on the spot: qualifying long-term holiday products carry a 14-day withdrawal right under the 2010 Regulations. Report suspected fraud to Report Fraud or Police Scotland on 101.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What is a holiday club scam?

A holiday club scam is a scheme where fraudsters or unscrupulous operators pose as legitimate holiday membership companies, offering access to cheap holidays, luxury resorts, or exclusive travel deals. In reality, they pressure you into signing expensive long-term contracts with hidden fees, poor-quality accommodation, or no real holidays at all. Some scammers collect upfront fees and disappear entirely. Others lock you into annual membership costs that are far higher than advertised, with cancellation clauses that make it nearly impossible to leave.

The scam preys on people's desire for affordable holidays and their trust in what appears to be a professional travel company. Victims often discover too late that the promised holidays are unavailable, the resorts are substandard, or the contract terms are completely different from what was verbally promised. The financial damage can be substantial, with some victims paying thousands of pounds over several years before realising they have been defrauded.

How holiday club scammers make first contact

Holiday club scammers typically reach you through multiple channels designed to feel legitimate and urgent. You may receive a cold call claiming you have won a free holiday or been selected for an exclusive travel membership offer. Others arrive via email or text message with similar claims, often with a link to a professional-looking website. Some scammers use high-pressure tactics, telling you the offer is only valid for a limited time or that you must attend a presentation to claim your prize.

They may also target you at holiday fairs, travel expos, or shopping centres, where they set up booths offering free holiday vouchers in exchange for your details. Once they have your contact information, they escalate the pressure, inviting you to a 'free' presentation or consultation where trained sales staff use aggressive tactics to push you into signing a contract on the spot. The entire process is designed to move quickly — from initial contact to signed contract — before you have time to research the company or seek independent advice.

Red flags that should stop you signing

  • Pressure to sign a contract immediately or within a very short timeframe, with claims that the offer expires today or this week.
  • Vague descriptions of what holidays you actually get access to, or refusal to provide a written list of available resorts and dates.
  • High upfront fees (often £1,000 to £5,000 or more) described as a 'membership fee', 'registration fee', or 'deposit', with promises you will recoup it through savings.
  • Annual membership costs that are significantly higher than the initial quote, or hidden fees buried in the small print of the contract.
  • Difficulty getting a clear written breakdown of all costs, cancellation terms, and what is actually included in the membership.
  • Testimonials or reviews that are vague, undated, or only available on the company's own website, with no independent verification on trusted review sites.
  • Reluctance to provide contact details for previous customers you can verify independently, or claims that customer details are confidential.
  • A sales team that dismisses your questions or concerns, or uses emotional manipulation ('this is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity') rather than factual information.

How to verify if a holiday club is genuine

Before you commit to any holiday club membership, take these verification steps. First, search the company name online alongside words like 'scam', 'complaint', or 'review' — check independent review sites such as Trustpilot and Which?, and your nation's consumer service website, for any warnings or complaints. Second, you can check whether the company belongs to ABTA – The Travel Association (formerly the Association of British Travel Agents) or holds an ATOL licence from the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) — but treat this as a useful extra check, not a pass/fail test.

ABTA membership is voluntary, and ATOL is generally required for flight-inclusive packages and can also be required for certain flight-only sales, though exemptions apply — a holiday-club membership with no flight component may fall outside the scheme. Most holiday club and long-term holiday product memberships aren't "package holidays" at all — they're covered separately, under the Timeshare, Holiday Products, Resale and Exchange Contracts Regulations 2010 — so a genuine holiday club can legitimately hold neither ABTA membership nor an ATOL licence, and their absence alone isn't a reliable sign of a scam for this type of product.

Third, request a full written contract at least 14 days before you sign anything, and take it to a solicitor or the consumer service for your nation for independent review — never sign at a presentation or under time pressure. Fourth, contact previous customers directly (ask the company for contact details and verify them independently) and ask about their actual experience, costs, and whether they have been able to use the holidays as promised.

Fifth, check the company's physical address and phone number — call the number yourself using a number from their official website, not one provided by a salesman. Scammers often use virtual offices or shared addresses. Finally, be extremely wary of any company that cannot or will not provide clear, written answers to your questions about costs and cancellation terms.

What to do immediately if you have already signed

If you have signed a long-term holiday product contract and now have doubts, act quickly. The 2010 Regulations can provide a 14-day withdrawal period for contracts within their scope, including qualifying long-term holiday products, but not every holiday booking or membership is covered. Check the contract and the statutory information, and ask the consumer service for your nation or a solicitor if unsure. Do not authorise any new or unexpected payment.

Before stopping a scheduled contractual instalment, get consumer or legal advice and formally exercise any withdrawal right that applies — cancelling the payment instruction alone does not end the contract. Contact the bank or card provider promptly about any unauthorised or fraudulent payment, keep the contract and messages, and report suspected fraud to Report Fraud. Report Fraud covers England, Wales and Northern Ireland. If you live in Scotland or the crime happened there, contact Police Scotland on 101.

Reporting a holiday club scam in the UK

If you believe you have been targeted by or fallen victim to a holiday club scam, report it through multiple official channels to maximise the chance of action. Start by reporting to Report Fraud, the fraud reporting service for England, Wales and Northern Ireland, either by calling 0300 123 2040 or submitting a report online at reportfraud.police.uk. In Scotland, contact Police Scotland on 101 instead.

Provide as much detail as possible: the company name, website, phone number, email address, names of staff members you spoke to, dates of contact, and a description of what happened and how much money you lost. Forward a suspicious email to the NCSC Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk. You can forward a suspicious SMS text to 7726 free of charge; use the relevant built-in reporting tool for RCS, iMessage and app messages.

You should also report the matter to the consumer service for your nation — Citizens Advice in England and Wales on 0808 223 1133, Advice Direct Scotland in Scotland on 0808 800 9060, or Consumerline in Northern Ireland on 0300 123 6262 — which can advise on your rights and may pass relevant complaint information to Trading Standards or another appropriate enforcement body. If you paid by credit card, contact your card provider's fraud team immediately and request a chargeback.

If you paid by bank transfer, contact your bank's fraud team and ask whether the mandatory APP reimbursement rules cover the payment; eligibility and exclusions depend on the payment type and circumstances. Keep copies of all reports and reference numbers for your records.

Can you get your money back?

Recovery depends on the contract, payment method and evidence. Card chargeback time limits are set by the card scheme and vary; ask the issuer promptly rather than relying on a fixed number. A qualifying UK Faster Payments or CHAPS transfer made on or after 7 October 2024 may fall under the PSR’s APP reimbursement rules, subject to scope, exclusions and claim deadlines. A 14-day withdrawal right may apply to a qualifying long-term holiday product, not automatically to every holiday club or booking. Keep all evidence and obtain consumer or legal advice for a disputed contract.

Frequently asked questions

How do I know if a holiday club company is real or a scam?

You can check whether the company belongs to ABTA – The Travel Association or holds an ATOL licence, but treat that as one factor among several rather than a decisive test — ABTA membership is voluntary and most holiday club memberships aren't package holidays, so a genuine operator may hold neither. Search the company and its directors independently, read review-platform feedback cautiously, and look for regulator or consumer warnings. Ask for a full written contract at least 14 days before signing. Ask a solicitor to review the contract if legal review is needed; your nation's consumer service can explain your consumer rights and possible next steps. Be very suspicious of any company that pressures you to sign immediately, cannot provide clear written details of costs and cancellation terms, or refuses to let you contact previous customers independently.

I signed a holiday club contract last week — can I cancel it?

A qualifying long-term holiday product can have a 14-day withdrawal period under the 2010 Regulations, even if signed in person. The right does not automatically cover every holiday membership or booking. Check the contract and send written notice promptly if the Regulations apply; contact your nation's consumer service if the position is unclear.

What should I do if I have already paid money to a holiday club scam?

Stop further payments and contact the bank or card provider promptly. Ask about chargeback or, for a qualifying UK bank transfer made on or after 7 October 2024, the PSR APP reimbursement rules. Eligibility and deadlines apply. Report suspected fraud and keep the contract, messages, receipts and payment details.

Is there a way to check if a holiday club website is fake?

Look for several warning signs: poor spelling or grammar, a generic or recently registered domain name, no clear company address or phone number, no independent reviews or only reviews on their own website, and pressure to enter payment details or sign up immediately. Check the website's domain registration using a WHOIS lookup tool — scam sites often use recently registered domains or hide their registration details. If the website looks professional but you are still unsure, do not enter any personal or payment details; instead, contact the company using a phone number from their official website (not from an email or text message) and ask questions about their registration and credentials.

What if I attended a holiday club presentation and was pressured into signing?

You still have consumer rights. If the agreement is a timeshare, qualifying long-term holiday product, resale or exchange contract within the Timeshare, Holiday Products, Resale and Exchange Contracts Regulations 2010, and you signed within the last 14 days, you generally have a withdrawal period and can cancel by giving written notice citing those Regulations. Not every holiday booking or membership is covered, so check the contract and the statutory information first. Keep proof of what you sent and when; recorded delivery is one way to do that, not the only valid route. If you were misled about what was included, the costs, or the cancellation terms, you may have grounds to claim under consumer protection law. For free advice on your specific situation contact the service for your nation — Citizens Advice in England and Wales on 0808 223 1133, Advice Direct Scotland in Scotland on 0808 800 9060, or Consumerline in Northern Ireland on 0300 123 6262 — or report the matter to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. Do not authorise any new or unexpected payment while you are investigating your options. Before stopping a scheduled contractual instalment, take consumer or legal advice and formally exercise any withdrawal right that applies — cancelling the payment instruction alone does not end the contract.
